title: One cell, one rule, no pattern
hook: One live cell, one tiny rule for every cell. Does a simple rule draw a tidy picture?

knows: a Game of Life grid updates by a neighbour rule (glider-walks)
doesNotKnow: that a one-row rule with three-cell neighbourhoods can look random from a single cell

misconception: A rule that treats every cell the same, started from a single cell, gives a simple tidy pattern.
objective: The learner can explain that Rule 30 and Rule 90 both start from one live cell and update every cell by the same three-cell rule, yet after 8 steps Rule 90 has a tidy nested triangle with 2 live cells in the row while Rule 30 has 7 and an irregular pattern, so a simple uniform rule need not give a simple picture.

claims.text: Rule 90's row 8 had 2 live cells, in a neat nested triangle. Rule 30's had 7, and its counts went 1, 3, 3, 6, 4, 9, 5, 12, 7.
claims.source: Demo.tsx grow(); builder's node script (2026-10-14): next cell = bit (left*4 + self*2 + right) of the rule number, 17-cell row, dead beyond the edges (the pattern is 2*8 + 1 = 17 wide at step 8, so the edge is never involved). Rule 30 counts 1, 3, 3, 6, 4, 9, 5, 12, 7; Rule 90 counts 1, 2, 2, 4, 2, 4, 4, 8, 2 (Rule 90 from one cell is Pascal's triangle mod 2, the Sierpinski pattern; row 8 has 2 live cells because C(8, k) is odd only for k = 0 and 8). Matches the brief and spec. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): Numbers re-run (Demo.tsx grow(), 17-cell row): Rule 30 counts 1,3,3,6,4,9,5,12,7, Rule 90 row 8 = 2. DISPUTED: the reveal sentence this claim records says the counts went '1, 3, 3, 6, 4, 9, 5, 12, 7 with no pattern', and the shown counts have an obvious one (odd steps 3, 6, 9, 12; even steps rise 1, 3, 4, 5, 7). The run breaks only at step 9 (12, not 15). Fix: drop 'with no pattern', or say the run does not last (step 9 gives 12, step 10 gives 11). | CLAIM FIX 2026-10-14 (demo-builder, W-197): Reveal no longer says 'with no pattern'; it now ends at the counts, matching this claim text. 'Breaks at step 9' not added because the stage stops at step 8. Also v2: grow() row typed number[] (TS2322), no behaviour change. Needs an independent check.

claims.text: Rule 30: 111→0, 110→0, 101→0, 100→1, 011→1, 010→1, 001→1, 000→0; Rule 90: a cell is alive if exactly one of its two neighbours is.
claims.source: Wolfram's numbering: the outputs for neighbourhoods 111, 110, ..., 000 read as a binary number give the rule number. 30 = 00011110 in binary; 90 = 01011010, which is left XOR right. S. Wolfram, 'Statistical mechanics of cellular automata', Reviews of Modern Physics 55 (1983) 601-644. Builder has not opened the paper in this session. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): verified. Re-derived: 30 = 00011110 gives 111..000 -> 0,0,0,1,1,1,1,0, matching the question and TILES; bit n of 90 equals left XOR right for all 8 neighbourhoods (node). Wolfram 1983 RMP not opened; the sentence depends only on the numbering, which is checked by computation.

claims.text: Rule 30 treats every cell the same, yet its right side turns irregular within a few rows, and no simple formula for its counts is known.
claims.source: Uniform update: by definition (c2). Irregular right side: visible in the builder's run (left edge a regular stripe, right side irregular). No known formula: Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (2002), ch. 2, discusses Rule 30's apparent randomness; in 2019 Wolfram posed open 'Rule 30 Prize Problems' (writings.stephenwolfram.com, 2019-10-01), including whether computing the nth centre cell needs about n steps. Builder has not opened these sources; a fact-checker should confirm the 'no formula for the counts' wording is supported. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): verified. Uniform update: by grow(). Irregular right side: 201-cell run to step 16 shows a regular stripe on the left edge and irregular triangles on the right. No known formula: OEIS A070952 (counts of 1s, Rule 30) lists the sequence, Mathematica/Haskell one-liners and the trivial relation a(n) = 2n+1 - A070951(n), no closed form (seen through a web-search extract; oeis.org itself blocked). Moderate confidence: 'not known' is an absence claim.

claims.text: A simple rule does not promise a simple picture.
claims.source: Generalisation from c1 and c3: Rule 30 is a counterexample to 'a uniform rule from a single cell gives a tidy pattern'. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): verified. Follows from c1 and c3 (counterexample).

claims.text: Its centre column read 110111001 against Rule 90's 100000000.
claims.source: Demo.tsx centre(); builder's node script (2026-10-14), steps 0..8, same rule code as c1. Matches the brief. Shown only if the learner turned the centre column on. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): verified. Re-ran: centre columns 110111001 (Rule 30) and 100000000 (Rule 90), steps 0-8.

claims.text: Rule 30's centre column has been used as a random number source in Mathematica.
claims.source: S. Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Wolfram Media, 2002), ch. 6 or 7 on randomness; the brief cites p. 317 and marks it 'check page before building'. The builder could not check the page; a fact-checker must open the book. Mathematica's documentation for Random / SeedRandom (Method -> "CellularAutomaton") is a second place to look. Shown only if the learner turned the centre column on. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): verified. NKS p. 317 (ch. 7, 'The Intrinsic Generation of Randomness'): web-search extract of wolframscience.com/nks/p317 says Mathematica's Random[Integer] has long produced its bits from the Rule 30 centre column; Wikipedia (Rule 30) and a Wolfram Demonstration agree. Page reached only through the search index (host blocked to fetch); no conflicting source.

recall.question: Two one-row rules both start from a single live cell and update every cell from itself and its two neighbours. What can you say about the pictures they make?
options: Both will be tidy, because every cell follows the same simple rule
One can be a neat nested triangle while the other looks random
Both will die out within a few steps
recall.why: Rule 90 builds a nested triangle, but Rule 30 from the same single cell gives irregular rows (row 8 has 7 live cells) with no simple pattern. A simple uniform rule does not promise a simple picture.
